corrected_value.title: The cocktail party phenomenon revisited: Attention and memory in the classic selective listening procedure of Cherry (1953).

decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The primary text explicitly retests Wood and Cowan (1995), which first introduced the online shadowing-error analysis across word positions around the presentation of one's own name (positions -1, 0, +1, +2, and +3) alongside retrospective name detection (35% vs. 29% here). Shipped row 144 (Moray, 1959, 10.1080/17470215908416289) is a distinct earlier study that measured only retrospective name detection and did not examine shadowing errors by word position; report equivalence does not apply.

corrected_value.authors: Conway AR, Cowan N, & Bunting MF
corrected_value.title: The cocktail party phenomenon revisited: The importance of working memory capacity.

decisions.quote:
Replicating the finding of
Conway et al. (2001)
that individual differences in working memory span are related to errors in shadowing after the presentation of one’s own name, low span participants were more likely than high span participants to commit shadowing errors on a relevant to-be-shadowed word location. While this was true regardless of whether participants were classified based on their operation span scores or based on their running span scores, the effect was largest when participants were classified based on both scores combined. Thus it seems the effect is most reliably detected when more than one measure of working memory span is used.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The study explicitly adopts the operation-span scoring and upper-versus-lower quartile comparison procedure of Conway et al. (2001) to retest whether low-span participants detect their own name more often and commit more shadowing errors at relevant word locations (word, word +1, word +2) than high-span participants. This independent 2001 individual-differences study is absent from shipped row 144 (Moray, 1959) and is distinct from sibling target 1 (Wood & Cowan, 1995).

corrected_value.authors: Röer JP, Bell R, Körner U, & Buchner A
corrected_value.title: A semantic mismatch effect on serial recall: Evidence for interlexical processing of irrelevant speech.

decisions.location: Discussion (chunk 38); see also Introduction (chunks 8-11), Results (chunks 21, 24), Discussion (chunk 35), and References (chunk 47)
decisions.reason: Röer and Cowan (2020/2021) review Röer, Bell, Körner, & Buchner (2019) in the Introduction (chunk 8) for the finding that semantically unexpected sentence-final words in irrelevant speech disrupt serial recall more than expected endings, and make testing whether semantically unexpected words are detected or disrupt shadowing in dichotic selective listening Purpose (1) of the study (chunk 11). They manipulate expected versus unexpected proverb endings within-subjects (N=80), find strong Bayesian evidence for the null on shadowing errors (BF10=0.060, chunk 24) and near-zero retrospective detection (1/80, chunk 21), and explicitly contrast their null findings with Röer et al. (2019) in the Discussion (chunks 35, 38), concluding that cross-modal distraction findings do not generalize to unimodal auditory selective listening. Primary abstract facts (0089) confirm Röer et al. (2019) reports 5 cross-modal serial-recall experiments establishing this semantic mismatch effect. Under the codebook, this cross-paradigm generalizability test is a conceptual replication absent from shipped row 144 (Moray, 1959).

decisions.quote:
Further work on adult aging by
Naveh-Benjamin et al. (2014)
shows that it is not low span per se that drives the individual difference in noticing one’s own name, but span insofar as it relates to control of attention. Specifically, while two thirds of the younger participants noticed their own name in the irrelevant message, older participants rarely did, even though their average span was equivalent to low-span young adults.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. Naveh-Benjamin et al. (2014) investigated adult aging differences in noticing one's own name (older vs. younger adults). The present study tested only a single young-adult sample (N = 80, M age = 25) and did not retest the aging finding of Naveh-Benjamin et al. (2014); its citation in the Introduction as a prior replication and in the Discussion as a literature reference rate for young adults in Experiments 1 and 4 is background context for the basic cocktail-party phenomenon already represented by shipped row 144 (Moray, 1959) and canonical missing targets 1 and 2.

Röer, Buchner, & Bell (in press) ('Auditory distraction in short-term memory: Stable effects of semantic mismatches on serial recall', Auditory Perception & Cognition 2(3), 143-162, print issue date 2019-07-03, online 2020-01-28, DOI 10.1080/25742442.2020.1722560) is co-cited once in the Introduction (chunk 8) alongside Röer et al. (2019) for the claim that semantically unexpected sentence endings disrupt serial recall more than expected endings, whereas the Discussion (chunk 35) cites only Röer et al. (2019). From the original-primary research context (0089), only metadata and a secondary indexed abstract were accessible for Röer, Buchner, & Bell (in press) (describing two experiments on nonhabituation/repetition of distractor sentences and citing Röer et al., 2019); its primary full text/methods were blocked (HTTP 403). Because the current study does not test habituation across repeated sentences and the primary report/cohort relationship between the 2019 and in-press papers remains unverified, whether target 5 is a distinct retested target cannot be determined.
